#9644. CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9643. Hyring Introduces Insight Workforce Intelligence Platform

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

SAN FRANCISCO, California, November 23rd, 2026/TechnologyWire/--Hyring, the AI hiring platform that has run more than 900,000 AI interviews, is now revolutionizing one of the oldest office practices: the timesheet. With Hyring Insight, employers can track work time and see where the day is actually going.

Conventional time tracking requires employees to remember and keep track of their work hours and managers to trust the data. Hyring Insight does things differently. Employees pick their start times, and that's when tracking begins. Once they finish their workday, they can stop the timer. Any meetings on Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet, Webex, and Slack huddles are detected and will be counted as meeting time without manual recording. If any time is missed, it can be submitted for approval with the reason.

“Nobody has ever created a company or a product because they loved filling out a timesheet every week,” said Adithyan RK, CEO, Hyring. “The timesheet came into existence because there was no better way at that time to validate and monitor a working day. But there is now. The timer keeps a record of time, and AI helps keep everyone informed about it.”

Enterprises can measure three things with Hyring Insight’s time tracking software: worked time, productivity, and activity. Productivity can be seen in the apps they use and the websites they surf, or Ask AI can go through the person's screenshots and give an analysis of work done.

Ask AI answers simple questions like, ‘What did I work on yesterday?’ or ‘What did the content team work on last month?’ and gives accurate data and charts. These conversations with Ask AI are completely confidential and stick to data without weighing in on any problem.

When there is suspicious activity, Hyring Insight instantly flags this and brings it to the admin's attention. This can include looking at unauthorized websites and unusual inputs caused by mouse activity that is being intentionally falsified, while only comparing the person's data with their previous data and never with a colleague. On the Pro and Enterprise plan, AI will explain why activity was flagged while objectively telling the admin what happened.

“Hours can always go either here or there,” said Adithyan RK, CEO, Hyring. “A manager never wants to know how many hours an employee worked; they want to know what got done and how time can be used more productively. When an AI gives data for this, the timesheet stops being relevant.”

“If AI is going to pinpoint data, that same data must be accessible to the employees too,” said Adithyan RK, CEO, Hyring. “There is a fine line between surveillance and intelligence, and the intention is to stay on the right side of it.”

Hyring Insight runs on a desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux with a web portal. Companies can start for free with up to two users or test Pro for 14 days with no credit card needed.

Hyring is an AI hiring platform headquartered in Chennai, India, founded in 2022 by Adithyan RK and Surya N. Its products include the AI Video Interviewer, AI Resume Screener, AI Phone Screener, AI Coding Interviewer, and English Proficiency Test, and the platform has completed 900,000 plus interviews for early-stage startups and Fortune 500 companies. Hyring Insight is its newest endeavor in workforce intelligence.Contact

#9642. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9641. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9640. 5 API Security Bugs That Slip Past Product Reviews (And How to Fix Them)

I am a Product Manager trying to bridge the gap between complex customer requirements and high-impact technical execution.

I am a Product Manager trying to bridge the gap between complex customer requirements and high-impact technical execution.

I am a Product Manager trying to bridge the gap between complex customer requirements and high-impact technical execution.

When an API gets breached, it’s rarely because an attacker found a zero-day exploit in your cloud provider’s load balancer. Usually, the API did the exact thing it was programmed to do: it took a request, saw a valid login token, ran a database query, and returned a 200 OK.

Automated security scanners are terrible at catching these bugs because scanners don't understand your product's business logic. They can't tell the difference between a user downloading their own invoice and a user downloading their competitor's invoice.

As a Product Manager, if you treat API design as an invisible engineering implementation detail, these logic gaps will ship to production. Here are five technical API bugs that routinely slip through sprint reviews, why they happen during normal feature work, and how to close them in both your PRDs and your architecture.

How it happens in a sprint: You’re shipping a feature that lets users export their monthly billing report. The acceptance criteria in the ticket says: "Logged-in users can click 'Download' to fetch their report via GET /api/v1/reports/{report_id}."

Engineering puts standard auth middleware on the route. The middleware checks that the user’s JWT signature is valid and not expired. Then the controller runs:

QA tests the happy path in staging, the download works, and the ticket gets closed.

The vulnerability: Your auth middleware checked who the caller was, but the query never checked if that caller actually owns report 9402. Any customer on a free trial can open Chrome DevTools, change 9402 to 9403, and pull another company's report. This is Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA), and it is still the #1 cause of API data leaks.

In the code: Never trust resource IDs from the URL alone. Pull the tenant_id or user_id directly from the verified JWT claims and force it into the data access layer:

In the PRD: Stop allowing sequential integer IDs (9401, 9402) in external URLs—require UUIDv4 or ULIDs so attackers can't loop through your database with a Python script. And write negative acceptance criteria explicitly: "User A with a valid token must receive a 403/404 when requesting a report_id belonging to Tenant B."

How it happens in a sprint: You’re building a collaboration view where users can see who else commented on a ticket. The UI design only shows each commenter's firstName and avatarUrl.

To avoid writing a net-new backend serializer and delaying the sprint, the developer reuses the existing User ORM model and returns the raw object: return res.json(user). The React frontend grabs the two fields it needs and ignores the rest.

The vulnerability: The UI looks clean, so it passes product sign-off. Meanwhile, the raw JSON payload sitting in the browser's Network tab is leaking user.email, user.phone, user.role, user.mfaEnabled, and user.stripeCustomerId for every user on the thread.

The reverse happens on PATCH and PUT routes (Mass Assignment). If the backend takes the incoming JSON body and passes it straight into User.update(req.body), a user can intercept their own profile-update request, inject "role": "admin" or "plan_tier": "enterprise" into the JSON payload, and overwrite columns they were never meant to touch.

How it happens in a sprint: You’re launching an SMS OTP login flow, a PDF export feature, or an AI summary button powered by an LLM API. During the security review, someone asks about rate limiting. DevOps confirms that Cloudflare or Nginx is already configured to block any IP address that exceeds 1,000 requests per minute. Everyone checks the box and moves on.

The vulnerability: A blanket 1,000 req/min IP limit protects your infrastructure from a basic DDoS, but it does nothing to protect your product logic or your cloud budget:

How it happens in a sprint: As the product scales from a monolith to microservices, the team puts an API Gateway at the edge to centralize authentication. The gateway verifies the user's JWT, extracts the user ID, strips the token, and forwards the request inside the VPC with a plaintext header like X-User-Id: 4821. Internal microservices trust that header implicitly because "it came from inside our private network."

The vulnerability: This creates a hard shell with a soft center. If an attacker finds a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) bug in a peripheral service—like a webhook tester, an image importer, or an outdated third-party library—they can trick that service into making internal HTTP requests across your cluster with any X-User-Id or X-Tenant-Id header they want, completely bypassing the API Gateway.

How it happens in a sprint: Your team rebuilds the checkout or user-management flow in /api/v2 with strict schema validation, better RBAC checks, and cleaner error handling.

When it’s time to turn off /api/v1, someone points out that an old iOS app build from 18 months ago—or one enterprise customer's custom webhook script—is still hitting the v1 routes. Nobody wants to deal with customer complaints, so PM and Eng agree to leave /api/v1 running quietly in the background.

The vulnerability: Six months later, nobody on the team remembers /api/v1 exists. It isn't included in new threat models, and when security patches are applied to v2 controllers, nobody backports them to v1. Yet that unmaintained v1 code is still wired directly into your live production database. When pentesters or attackers hit a wall on /api/v2/users/export, the very first thing they try is changing the URL to /api/v1/users/export or /api/beta/users/export.

Before you click "Sign Off" on a user story or approve an API-backed feature during sprint review, sit down with your tech lead and ask these three specific questions. Here is how to evaluate their answers:

New York City, USA, November 23rd, 2026/Chainwire/--Armitage, Wintermute’s onchain vault curation arm, and Superform today announced a collaboration that gives holders of tokenized NVIDIA, Tesla, Apple and five other stocks an option beyond holding or selling.

Armitage will curate Superform’s Earn Stocks strategies on Base. Built on SuperformOS, these strategies let holders use their tokenized stocks as collateral while keeping their stock exposure.

Holders deposit their tokenized stocks, which are used as collateral to borrow USDC. That USDC is then lent out when expected lending rates are higher than the cost of borrowing. Holders keep their stock exposure, and any additional return comes from the gap between the two rates.

SuperStocks is Superform's family of products built on tokenized equities and Earn Stocks is the strategy layer that puts the assets inside those products to work. Armitage’s role covers strategy design, allocation, risk management and ongoing monitoring.

SuperformOS provides the operating system behind the products, bringing automated strategy execution, rule-based risk controls, accounting, and redemptions onto shared, verifiable infrastructure.

“Putting a stock onchain is the starting point. The opportunity is building the financial products people use around it,” said Vikram Arun, CEO of Superform. “Superform brings together the infrastructure to run those products and the distribution to put them in investors’ hands. With Armitage, we’re bringing Wintermute’s strategy expertise into that system, starting with earning on stocks. Our ambition is to make SuperStocks the building blocks for a new generation of portfolios and investment products.”For us, the opportunity is giving holders more options than just holding or selling their tokenized stocks,” said Igor Igamberdiev, Armitage Lead. “Putting those stocks to use onchain comes with real risks. Stock prices move, borrowing rates change, and positions need to be watched closely. That is the work we do every day, and we’re glad to be doing it with Superform.”

The collaboration covers eight existing SuperStocks products: NVIDIA, SpaceX, Tesla, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Apple. Armitage is taking over as curator in stages, starting with the Amazon SuperVault (superAMZN). No new tokenized stocks are being issued.

Additional returns are variable and not guaranteed. Users can lose principal through market, borrowing-rate, liquidation, liquidity, oracle and smart-contract risks. Availability is subject to eligibility and applicable restrictions. This release is informational, not investment advice.

Eligible users can explore Earn Stocks and review SuperStocks product terms at https://app.superform.xyz/#stocks.

Superform is the neobank for global markets. Buy U.S. stocks, earn on USD, trade crypto, and send money without restrictions. Under the hood, SuperformOS connects financial products so users can move between investing, earning, and trading in fewer steps and earn more money, safely.

Armitage is Wintermute's onchain vault curation arm, designed to scale across protocols and chains as yield opportunities emerge across an expanding DeFi landscape. Corto Industries Limited, is a company registered in the Cayman Islands (Company No. MC-434730), hereafter referred to as “Armitage”.

#9635. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

#9632. Feature Flags at Scale: Architecture, Consistency, and Reliable Rollouts

Feature flags turn deployment into a reversible control decision rather than a one way release event. At small scale, that can look like a boolean wrapped around a new code path. At production scale, the mechanism becomes a distributed control system. Configuration has to propagate quickly, evaluation has to stay fast and available during network failures, targeting has to be deterministic, and every rollout has to be observable enough to stop before a partial regression turns into an incident across the whole fleet. OpenFeature describes flags as runtime decisions that can support canaries, experiments, degradation controls, and targeting based on context without a redeploy, and mature platforms separate flag management from evaluation at request time.

The most important scaling boundary is the separation between a control plane and an evaluation plane. The control plane stores flag definitions, targeting rules, rollout percentages, audit data, and administrative state. The evaluation plane answers the application’s immediate question, which is which variation applies to this request. A synchronous network call from every request to a central flag service makes that service part of the application’s latency and availability budget, so production grade SDKs usually cache configuration and evaluate locally. LaunchDarkly documents server side SDKs that retrieve flag state, keep it in memory, and evaluate locally. Unleash similarly describes backend SDKs that cache configuration and apply activation strategies inside the application process.

The resulting application code should stay intentionally boring. Flag evaluation belongs near the decision point, while business behavior stays in ordinary methods.

The fallback value is not cosmetic. LaunchDarkly states that an SDK returns the fallback defined by the application when initialization has not finished, the flag is missing, or initialization fails. After a successful initialization, cached state can keep serving evaluations during a loss of connectivity. That behavior makes flag evaluation a local dependency with remote configuration, rather than a remote dependency on every transaction.

Percentage rollout sounds probabilistic, but randomness on every request is usually the wrong implementation. A customer sent to the new checkout on one request and the old checkout on the next ends up with inconsistent state, noisy metrics, and hard to debug behavior. Mature systems instead hash a stable targeting key into a bucket and compare that bucket with the rollout threshold. OpenFeature explicitly defines a targeting key that identifies the subject of an evaluation, and notes that providers may require it for fractional evaluation. Unleash documents the same stability property and calls it stickiness. Raising a rollout percentage keeps the users already included and adds new ones, as long as the grouping input and context stay stable.

A simplified implementation captures the core idea without vendor specific behavior.

A threshold of 500 basis points exposes roughly five percent of the keyed population, and the same customer stays in the same cohort across requests. The exact hashing algorithm matters because changing it reshuffles exposure. LaunchDarkly and Unleash both treat cohort stability as part of rollout semantics, so hashing inputs and algorithm versions should be handled as compatibility sensitive data rather than incidental implementation details.

A safe flag system needs two properties that pull against each other. Configuration changes should arrive quickly, yet a temporary loss of the configuration service should not break request processing. Streaming updates are a common answer. LaunchDarkly documents a model in which SDKs load current state, keep a streaming connection open, and receive incremental targeting changes. If the connection drops, the SDK keeps the last known flag values while it tries to reconnect. Unleash uses local caches with periodic configuration refreshes and accepts a short propagation delay in exchange for local evaluation and resilience.

That design creates an explicit consistency model. Flag configuration is not instantaneous everywhere. It is eventually propagated to evaluators. The operational question becomes whether stale configuration is safer than unavailable evaluation. For most release flags, the last known good state is preferable because it preserves behavior that was previously valid. For emergency kill switches, propagation latency becomes part of incident response design, so streaming, edge relays, or tightly tuned refresh intervals may be justified. Martin Fowler’s distinction between release toggles and operational toggles reinforces this difference. Operational controls need much faster reconfiguration because their whole purpose is a rapid response in production.

A percentage slider alone does not make a rollout safe. Exposure should be tied to health signals that can halt further expansion or trigger a rollback. AWS AppConfig formalizes this pattern through deployment strategies with growth rates, deployment windows, bake times, and CloudWatch alarms. An alarm during a deployment can automatically restore the previous configuration. LaunchDarkly also documents guarded rollouts that monitor selected metrics and can roll back when they detect a regression.

The architectural implication is significant. Evaluation telemetry has to carry enough identity to connect application outcomes to flag decisions. OpenFeature’s observability guidance maps evaluation details such as the flag key and variant into telemetry attributes, and its hook model allows logging or telemetry logic around the evaluation lifecycle. At scale, this makes it possible to compare error rate, latency, saturation, conversion, or business specific failure metrics between exposed and unexposed cohorts without scattering custom instrumentation across every call site.

Feature flags reduce release risk by adding temporary branches to production code, but those branches are not free. Every long lived flag increases the number of possible runtime states and adds to testing, debugging, and operational complexity. Fowler explicitly describes flags as inventory with a carrying cost and recommends actively retiring flags that are no longer needed. The distinction matters because a release flag that survives long after full rollout quietly becomes permanent architecture.

A platform that scales therefore needs lifecycle metadata as much as targeting metadata. Ownership, creation time, intended removal date, rollout state, and last evaluation time let automation find stale flags and keep cleanup from becoming optional maintenance. Static analysis can locate flag keys in the source, while runtime telemetry can identify flags that are always true, always false, or no longer evaluated. The final removal should delete both the dead branch and the remote configuration so the codebase returns to a single authoritative path.

Feature flags scale safely when they are treated as a distributed release control system rather than as scattered conditionals. The strongest architecture keeps evaluation local at request time, propagates configuration asynchronously, assigns cohorts deterministically, survives control plane failures with explicit fallbacks, ties rollout progress to production telemetry, and retires temporary branches once the release is complete. Those properties separate a convenient toggle mechanism from reliable production infrastructure. At sufficient scale, the central design goal is not only the ability to turn functionality on and off. It is the ability to change production exposure quickly while preserving latency, consistency, observability, and reversibility under failure.

Distributed Locks Are More Dangerous Than They Look

#9631. The Handoff Is the Product: Where an AI Agent Should Stop and a Person Should Take Over

Posted on Nov 24 • Originally published at Medium • AI-assisted

By Shawn Carter, Manager at Autoesta. We build AI agents, CRM systems and automations for service businesses.

Most of the questions we get about AI agents are about the model. Which one is smartest, which one sounds most human on a call, which one is cheapest per message. Those are fair questions. In our view they are not the ones that decide whether an agent helps a business or embarrasses it.

What decides it is the handoff: the exact moment the agent stops and a person takes over, and what that person receives when they do. We now write the handoff rules before we write a single prompt. This piece explains why, and what those rules look like.

Picture an agent that handles nine messages in ten well and fumbles the tenth. That tenth message is where the angry customer, the refund, the legal question and the big deal sit. Those are the conversations a business can least afford to fumble.

The research we trust most points the same way. In "Generative AI at Work" (NBER working paper 31161), Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond studied 5,179 customer support agents who were given an AI assistant in stages. Issues resolved per hour rose about 14 percent on average, and the biggest gains went to newer, less experienced staff. That study measured AI helping people, not AI replacing them. The lesson we take from it is that the best results come from a person and a system working the same conversation, with a clean line between them.

So when a client asks "how much of this can the agent do alone?", our honest answer is: less than you think at launch, more over time, and only as fast as the handoff earns trust.

These are the rules we set on every build, whatever the channel (phone, SMS, WhatsApp, web chat or Instagram DMs).

1. The customer asks for a person. Words like "speak to someone", "real person", "complaint" or "refund" end the AI's turn. We don't let the agent argue, try once more, or ask "are you sure?". The cost of a frustrated customer is far higher than the cost of a staff member reading a message.

2. The answer isn't in the approved content. An agent should answer only from information the business has signed off: services, hours, policies, prices it is allowed to quote. When the question falls outside that, the right reply is "let me get someone who can answer that properly", not a confident guess. A made-up refund policy or price is the classic agent mistake, and it is completely avoidable.

3. The action is hard to undo. Booking a slot is easy to fix. Sending a message to a whole list, issuing a refund, changing a payment or deleting a record is not. Our rule: the agent can prepare those actions, but a person approves them. Fixed, rule-based steps (invoices, eligibility checks, compliance steps) stay in plain workflows where the same input always gives the same result. The agent handles the parts where the input varies and judgment helps.

4. The lead is hot. This one surprises people. When a lead says they want to buy, book a large job or talk pricing for a big project, the agent's job is to get a person on the conversation quickly, not to close the deal itself. The agent qualifies, routes and books; people sell the conversations that matter most.

A handoff that drops the customer into a staff inbox with no context is barely better than no agent at all. The customer has to repeat themselves, and the staff member starts cold.

Every handoff we build passes on four things:

In GoHighLevel this usually means a tag, a note on the contact, an assigned owner and an alert to the right person. In other systems it's the same idea in different fields. The tools matter less than the rule: the person picks up exactly where the agent left off.

Voice agents need extra care. In February 2024 the FCC ruled that AI-generated voices count as "artificial" voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, so outbound AI calls need the same prior consent as prerecorded calls. That doesn't make AI calling off limits. It means inbound answering, confirmations and calls to people who asked to hear from you are a very different risk from cold outbound dialling. We treat consent records as part of the build, not an afterthought.

Our view is simple: start with the jobs where a wrong answer is cheap and a slow answer is expensive.

Missed calls are the best example. One of the businesses we work with, a handyman and property maintenance company, runs a missed-call auto reply so a new customer who calls during a job gets a text back instead of silence. A slightly imperfect text is far better than a voicemail nobody returns until evening. Lead routing is another: a personal training gym we built for gets enquiries from Yelp, Facebook lead ads, Google lead forms, its website and Mindbody, and the system's first job is making sure each one reaches the right coach.

Neither of those needs an agent to be brilliant. They need it to be fast, polite and clear about when it hands over.

The jobs we push later are the ones where mistakes are costly: quoting complex prices, handling disputes, anything regulated. Those come once the business has seen weeks of real conversations and trusts where the agent's limits are.

If you're comparing AI agent vendors or builders, these questions tell you more than any demo:

A builder who answers these quickly has done this before. One who talks only about the model probably hasn't thought about that tenth message yet.

AI agents are worth building for most service businesses we talk to. The value comes from a system that answers instantly, does the repetitive part well, and knows exactly when to step aside. Get the handoff right and the model choice becomes a detail.

If you want to see how we set up qualification and handoff rules, Autoesta publishes how its agents are built, including how its lead qualification agent scores and routes new enquiries (autoesta.com/ai-lead-qualification-agent).

Shawn Carter is a Manager at Autoesta, a 16-person team that builds AI agents, automations and CRM systems for service businesses.

#9629. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9628. Correctif virtuel vs application de correctifs : quand protéger une API plutôt que de redéployer

Posted on Nov 24 • Originally published at apidog.com

Le correctif virtuel bloque temporairement un chemin d'accès connu vers une faille logicielle, tandis que le code vulnérable reste en place. Recourez-y lorsque vous pouvez couvrir le trafic API concerné plus tôt que vous ne pouvez déployer un correctif en toute sécurité. Corrigez et vérifiez le parc concerné dès que la version corrigée est disponible.

Le 23 novembre 2026, OpenAI et Cisco ont présenté Shirudo, un projet Linux open source capable de charger des protections eBPF ciblées sur un système en cours d'exécution. Cela met en lumière une décision classique d'astreinte. Si le correctif définitif demande des heures de validation, pouvez-vous réduire l'exposition dès maintenant sans casser les requêtes dont vos clients dépendent ? Annonce de Shirudo par OpenAI

Un correctif virtuel est un contrôle compensatoire. Votre inventaire continue d'afficher la version vulnérable tant que le contrôle est actif. Laissez le ticket de remédiation ouvert et y consigner la règle, le responsable et la date de retrait prévue. Recommandations de l'OWASP sur le correctif virtuel

Un correctif classique peut être une bibliothèque mise à jour dans une image de conteneur ou une version corrigée de votre propre service. Suivez ce que le parc exécute réellement. Une image corrigée dans le registre ne dit pas grand-chose des anciens workers qui servent encore des requêtes. Guide de gestion des correctifs d'entreprise du NIST

Utilisez un bouclier lorsque trois conditions sont réunies.

Imaginons qu'une API d'objets ait une fonctionnalité de traitement optionnelle vulnérable, et que la passerelle permette déjà de désactiver l'accès à cette fonctionnalité. Votre équipe peut évaluer rapidement le comportement désactivé pendant qu'elle reconstruit et teste le service. Les lectures de collection et de détail devraient continuer à fonctionner. Si des clients utilisent la fonctionnalité optionnelle, informez le support de la réponse que ces clients recevront et de la durée probable de la modification.

Mesurez les deux côtés du compromis. Comparez le temps attendu pour appliquer la règle avec le temps nécessaire pour déployer une version corrigée sur le même ensemble de charges de travail. Surveillez le taux de réussite des requêtes normales, la latence et le nombre de rejets pendant le déploiement. Une hausse des rejets demande du contexte. Il peut s'agir du contrôle qui fait son travail, ou d'un flux client que vos fixtures de préproduction n'ont pas couvert.

Privilégiez un correctif immédiat lorsque la version corrigée est prête, qu'un canary semble sain et que le déploiement atteint les instances exposées aussi vite que la règle temporaire. Si aucun contrôle fiable ne couvre le chemin concerné et que le risque justifie une action immédiate, envisagez de restreindre l'accès ou de désactiver la capacité concernée pendant la préparation du correctif. En cas de preuve de compromission, lancez la réponse à incident en parallèle de la remédiation.

Choisissez le point d'application en fonction de ce qu'il peut observer et des requêtes qui doivent le traverser. Un pare-feu d'application web (WAF) au niveau d'une passerelle API y évalue le trafic HTTP. Un bouclier d'exécution Linux applique la politique là où l'hôte peut observer l'activité concernée. Chacun dépend de la couverture à sa propre couche.

Une règle de passerelle convient à une modification côté HTTP lorsque la passerelle voit les attributs de requête pertinents et que toutes les requêtes concernées la traversent. Vérifiez le périmètre par rapport à votre inventaire de services. Si un service traite des requêtes provenant de plusieurs sources, incluez ces chemins dans votre plan de remédiation. Pour un exemple concret de l'importance de l'inventaire des composants, voir notre article sur une vulnérabilité RCE dans Brotli pour Node.js.

Un contrôle hôte se justifie lorsque le comportement concerné est visible sur l'hôte et que vous pouvez établir une couverture sur les noyaux et charges de travail concernés. Son emplacement peut rapprocher le contrôle du composant que vous protégez, avec ses propres exigences de déploiement et de retour arrière. Conservez les contrôles d'autorisation applicative dans le plan de tests de mise en production. Une modification de passerelle doit faire l'objet de la même revue que toute modification d'autorisation de middleware.

Shirudo peut charger des protections eBPF ciblées sur un système Linux en cours d'exécution sans le redémarrer pour appliquer le bouclier. OpenAI décrit un flux de travail assisté par agent pour préparer et vérifier un bouclier candidat, les opérateurs contrôlant le déploiement. Le projet décrit des chargeurs signés pour les protections BPF, une vérification par le noyau et des preuves ancrées dans le TPM des modifications apportées aux protections chargées. Dépôt Shirudo

Le dépôt indique que le projet est en pré-version. Il liste un noyau Linux avec l'ABI des chargeurs signés et les correctifs du noyau Shirudo, ainsi que TPM 2.0, pour les cibles de production. OpenAI présente l'identification et le déploiement à l'échelle de l'organisation comme un objectif à long terme. Prévoyez un budget distinct pour la préparation des hôtes et la revue d'une modification temporaire. Description par OpenAI de la feuille de route de Shirudo

Examinez un bouclier proposé comme une modification de production, même s'il n'a fallu que quelques minutes pour le rédiger. La signature établit la provenance lorsque vous faites confiance au signataire. La vérification à l'exécution contrôle le programme par rapport aux règles de sécurité applicables. Votre propre revue doit encore établir si la politique correspond aux charges de travail visées, préserve le trafic normal et dispose d'un plan de retrait.

Retirez un bouclier temporaire après avoir vérifié que la version corrigée couvre le parc concerné et que le service corrigé réussit ses contrôles de mise en production. Conservez un responsable et une date de revue sur le ticket d'incident jusqu'à ce que le retrait soit terminé. Si la couverture est incomplète, notez quels systèmes ont encore besoin d'une atténuation et qui en est responsable.

Décidez de ce qui se passe si le correctif est annulé. Si vous revenez à une version affectée, maintenez ou rétablissez la protection correspondante avant que cette version ne reçoive du trafic. Traitez le déploiement du code et le retrait de la règle comme deux modifications distinctes afin que l'équipe puisse vérifier chacune d'elles.

Utilisez votre agent de codage et Apidog CLI pour transformer un inventaire d'endpoints en liste de vérification de préproduction. Pour l'API d'objets, commencez par la lecture de collection et la lecture de détail. Conservez les mêmes fixtures pour la ligne de base, la version de préproduction protégée et la version de préproduction corrigée afin que les comparaisons soient pertinentes.

Installez la CLI et connectez-vous avec votre jeton d'accès API Apidog. Indiquez à l'agent votre ID de projet. Si vous travaillez dans Codex, suivez la configuration d'Apidog CLI pour Codex.

L'agent exécute cette commande d'inventaire en lecture seule.

Dans la sortie du sandbox, GET /objects et GET /objects/{id} donnent à l'agent deux contrôles distincts à proposer. Pour la collection, utilisez une liste préremplie et vérifiez le statut attendu ainsi que la forme de la réponse. Pour le détail, utilisez un ID de fixture connu et vérifiez que la réponse correspond à cette fixture. Comparez les résultats de préproduction et signalez toute modification de contrat avant de poursuivre. L'inventaire indique quelles requêtes couvrir. Des tests réussis sur le service en préproduction fournissent la preuve nécessaire au déploiement. Une fois que vous disposez d'une suite réutilisable, joignez ses résultats à la tâche de mise en production. Apidog CLI dans les pipelines CI/CD

Si les réviseurs API et infrastructure travaillent séparément, attribuez la liste de vérification de l'agent et la revue du bouclier comme deux tâches distinctes dans Sharkly. Cela permet à votre équipe de confier du travail à des agents de codage sur vos propres ordinateurs et d'examiner leurs résultats avant le déploiement.

Les termes peuvent se recouper. Le correctif virtuel décrit l'objectif d'un contrôle temporaire qui bloque l'accès à une faille. Le correctif à chaud décrit la manière dont une modification prend effet sur un système en cours d'exécution. Une modification à chaud peut appliquer une restriction temporaire à l'exécution ou mettre à jour du code en cours d'exécution, selon l'outil.

Non. Choisissez un contrôle qui voit le comportement concerné et couvre les charges de travail affectées. Un WAF convient au trafic HTTP au niveau d'une passerelle. Un contrôle à l'exécution peut convenir à l'activité au niveau de l'hôte. Si votre équipe peut livrer un correctif vérifié dans le même délai, le correctif définitif peut être l'opération la plus simple.

Conservez-le jusqu'à ce que vous ayez vérifié le correctif définitif sur l'ensemble du parc concerné. Fixez une date de revue lors de l'activation du bouclier et réexaminez-la si le déploiement prend du retard. Un parc aux versions hétérogènes peut nécessiter le bouclier plus longtemps que le premier déploiement réussi.

Utilisez votre processus de contrôle des modifications pour décider qui approuve le déploiement. Pour le flux Shirudo décrit par OpenAI, les agents peuvent aider à préparer et valider les protections, et les équipes de sécurité contrôlent ce qui est déployé. Fournissez aux réviseurs le périmètre cible, les résultats de validation et les instructions de retrait.

Consignez l'atténuation et son périmètre, puis laissez la remédiation définitive ouverte. Joignez les preuves des versions corrigées et les résultats de vérification lorsque le déploiement est terminé. Le suivi des deux modifications permet à l'équipe d'astreinte de voir si elle peut retirer le bouclier en toute sécurité.
